extracted.intended_audience: general readers, aspiring novelists, and students of Victorian prose / literary memoir
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and authorial reflections on producing novels and autobiographical prose — covering habits, style, plausibility, productivity, and the emotional conditions for writing. The page is an autobiographical excerpt (Trollope) that embeds prescriptive remarks about writing and literary practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintaining plausibility and unity in fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: "binding myself down to certain laws, to certain proportions, and proprieties, and unities. Nothing impossible was ever introduced,--nor even anything which, from outward circumstances, would seem to be violently improbable."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sustain internal consistency, proportions, and unities in a created tale; avoid introducing impossible events or occurrences that are wildly improbable given the story's setup. This is presented as a deliberate discipline the author used while inventing and sustaining long fictional narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to lay aside the author's identity
rubrics_metrics.description: "I have... been able to lay my own identity aside."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful fiction requires the writer to set aside personal selfhood and inhabit other characters and perspectives. This enables verisimilitude and prevents stories from being merely thinly-disguised autobiography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustained imaginative practice ('castle-building')
rubrics_metrics.description: The author describes always 'going about with some castle in the air firmly built within my mind' and carrying on the same tale 'for weeks, for months, if I remember rightly, from year to year.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular, prolonged imaginative play (inventing and developing stories over long periods) trains a writer to maintain interest in a fictitious story and to work to fixed laws and proportions. Trollope calls it a 'dangerous mental practice' but credits it with helping him become a novelist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular journal-keeping to build facility
rubrics_metrics.description: "At the age of fifteen, I had commenced the dangerous habit of keeping a journal... They habituated me to the rapid use of pen and ink, and taught me how to express myself with facility."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keeping a journal regularly develops writing fluency, quickness with pen and ink, and the ability to express ideas clearly — practical training for a fiction writer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional composure and suitability for novel-writing
rubrics_metrics.description: "I do not think that the writing of a novel is the most difficult task which a man may be called upon to do; but it is a task that may be supposed to demand a spirit fairly at ease."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A relative emotional steadiness or peace of mind is generally conducive to writing novels; severe emotional turmoil can impede or even 'kill' a writer's capacity to complete sustained fiction (illustrated by Sir Walter Scott).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity to separate practical cares from creative intellect
rubrics_metrics.description: "Her power of dividing herself into two parts, and keeping her intellect by itself clear from the troubles of the world, and fit for the duty it had to do..." (speaking of his mother writing while nursing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The practical skill of mentally separating domestic/emotional burdens from the creative mind enables one to continue productive literary work even under difficult circumstances — a valuable discipline and exception to the need for perfect tranquility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful diction and formality in polished correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenting on his mother's love-letters: 'They are, all of them, on square paper... the language in each, though it almost borders on the romantic, is beautifully chosen, and fit, without change of a syllable, for the most critical eye.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For polished letter-writing (and by extension refined prose), deliberate word-choice and an avoidance of slang or excessive familiarity contribute to elegance and lasting effect. The author contrasts this with more modern, casual usage which he thinks less conducive to poetic taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional regularity and reliable output
rubrics_metrics.description: Of his mother's practice: 'The novels went on, of course. We had already learned to know that they would be forthcoming at stated intervals,--and they always were forthcoming.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistency and punctuality in producing work (meeting intervals/deadlines) is presented as a professional virtue — particularly important when writing is a source of income.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding exaggeration; strive for accuracy in depiction
rubrics_metrics.description: "She was neither clear-sighted nor accurate; and in her attempts to describe morals, manners, and even facts, was unable to avoid the pitfalls of exaggeration."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing morals, manners, and facts, aim for clear-sightedness and accuracy; beware of the pitfalls of exaggeration which can weaken credibility or distort the material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of wide reading to inform literary judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: The author recounts reading Shakespeare, Byron, Scott, Miltonic lines, and other classics and using that knowledge in forming judgments (e.g., on best novels).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensive reading of literature across periods and authors cultivates taste, informs judgment about narrative form, and supplies models for style and structure; such reading compensates in part for gaps in formal schooling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid creating implausible, glorified heroes
rubrics_metrics.description: "I never became a king, or a duke... I never was a learned man... I was a very clever person..." (on how his boy-hero constructions remained plausible).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even in imaginative self-insertion, keep protagonists within believable social/physical/intellectual bounds rather than elevating them to improbable grandeur; believable heroes make more convincing fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical discipline and training matter more than competitive cramming
rubrics_metrics.description: On competitive examinations and preparation: competitive cramming 'has, I maintain, no connection whatever with education' and often 'fills [the candidate] with false ideas' of preparedness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For durable competence (whether in public service or analogous professional skills), practical learning, responsible mentorship, and true formative training trump short-term exam cramming. While not strictly a creative-writing rule, it bears on how one should be trained/prepared for professional literary life.
